questions.title: Route of spread, infiltrating breast carcinoma with axillary metastasis
questions.question: A 35-year-old female presented with a mass in the right breast adherent to the underlying structures, with enlarged firm axillary lymph nodes. Biopsy from the breast mass revealed malignant epithelial cells and biopsy from the enlarged lymph node showed the same neoplastic growth. What is the route of malignant spread in this case?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Blood spread alone does not explain the tumour being adherent to the underlying chest-wall structures, which reflects direct local extension.
explanations.B: Incorrect. There is no evidence here of a distant, blood-borne metastasis; the two sites involved (the breast itself and the draining axillary node) are exactly what direct-plus-lymphatic spread produces.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Direct spread alone explains the fixation to underlying structures but not the separate, biopsy-proven tumour in the axillary lymph node.
explanations.D: Correct. The mass is adherent to (fixed to) the underlying structures, showing direct local extension, and the enlarged axillary lymph node biopsy-proven to contain the same tumour shows lymphatic spread to the regional nodes draining the breast. Breast carcinoma classically spreads by this direct-plus-lymphatic combination before later blood-borne or other spread supervenes. Both criteria are explicitly satisfied by the vignette: fixation (direct) and nodal metastasis (lymphatic).
explanations.E: Incorrect. Transcoelomic spread applies to organs covered by serous membranes seeding a body cavity (e.g. ovary into the peritoneum), not to a breast mass with axillary nodal disease.

questions.learning_objective: Route of spread, infiltrating breast carcinoma with axillary metastasis

questions.title: Step of extracellular matrix invasion
questions.question: One of the following is a step included in the invasion of extracellular matrix by a malignant tumour cell:

explanations.A: Correct. Local invasion of the extracellular matrix begins with cell-cell detachment, the loss of adhesion molecules such as E-cadherin that frees an individual tumour cell from its neighbours. Only after this detachment can the cell attach to and degrade the matrix and migrate through it. It is therefore the first step of the local invasion cascade, occurring before the cell ever reaches a vessel.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Dissemination in circulation is a later step, occurring after the tumour cell has already invaded through the matrix and entered a vessel (intravasated).
explanations.C: Incorrect. Extravasation (exiting the vessel at a distant site) is a step of distant metastatic spread, occurring well after local matrix invasion.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Homing (localising to a specific distant organ) is one of the final steps of the metastatic cascade, not a step of local extracellular matrix invasion.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Intravasation (entry into a vessel) happens after the cell has already invaded through the matrix, not as part of that invasion step itself.

questions.learning_objective: Step of extracellular matrix invasion

questions.title: Microscopic picture of infiltrating malignant epithelial breast tumour
questions.question: For the same 35-year-old female with a breast mass adherent to underlying structures and malignant epithelial cells on biopsy, what is the expected microscopic picture of the breast lesion?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Adenoma is the benign tumour of glandular epithelium; the biopsy here shows malignant epithelial cells, ruling out a benign diagnosis.
explanations.B: Correct. Carcinoma is by definition the term for a malignant tumour of epithelial origin. The biopsy explicitly describes malignant epithelial cells, which is exactly the histogenetic category carcinoma names. Breast tissue is a glandular epithelial organ, so a malignant epithelial tumour arising there is a carcinoma, not a mesenchymal (sarcoma) or lymphoid (lymphoma) malignancy.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Lymphoma arises from lymphoid cells, not the malignant epithelial cells described in this breast biopsy.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Sarcoma is a malignant tumour of mesenchymal (connective tissue) origin, not the epithelial origin described here.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Papilloma is a benign tumour of protective epithelium, inconsistent with the malignant epithelial cells on biopsy.

questions.learning_objective: Microscopic picture of infiltrating malignant epithelial breast tumour

questions.title: Gross consistency of a malignant breast mass
questions.question: The excised malignant breast mass from this patient appears grossly:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Capsulation is a feature of benign tumours; a malignant tumour infiltrates surrounding tissue rather than being enclosed by a capsule.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Well-circumscribed margins describe a benign tumour's pushing border, not the poorly defined, infiltrative margin of a malignant tumour.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A fleshy, soft consistency is more typical of a sarcoma, not the classically firm/hard consistency of an infiltrating (scirrhous) breast carcinoma.
explanations.D: Correct. Malignant tumours, and infiltrating breast carcinoma in particular, are classically firm to hard on palpation and cut section, reflecting their dense fibrous (desmoplastic) stroma and infiltrative growth into surrounding tissue. This hard consistency is part of why such a mass is clinically detected as a hard, irregular lump. It contrasts with the soft, mobile feel typical of a benign lesion such as a fibroadenoma.
explanations.E: Incorrect. A soft consistency is typical of benign tumours (e.g. lipoma) or specific soft malignancies, not the classic hard consistency of infiltrating breast carcinoma.

questions.learning_objective: Gross consistency of a malignant breast mass

questions.title: Exception among benign-dangerous tumours
questions.question: The following list are benign dangerous tumours except:

explanations.A: Incorrect (this is a true benign-dangerous example, not the exception). A benign ureteric tumour is dangerous because it can obstruct urine flow despite being histologically benign.
explanations.B: Incorrect (true benign-dangerous example). A benign oesophageal tumour can obstruct the narrow oesophageal lumen and threaten swallowing/nutrition.
explanations.C: Incorrect (true benign-dangerous example). A benign cardiac tumour (e.g. myxoma, rhabdomyoma) can obstruct a valve or outflow tract and cause sudden cardiac compromise.
explanations.D: Incorrect (true benign-dangerous example). A pituitary adenoma is dangerous through mass effect on the optic chiasm and disruption of pituitary hormone axes, despite benign histology.
explanations.E: Correct. Lipoma, a benign fatty tumour typically arising in loose subcutaneous tissue (e.g. the forearm), sits in an accommodating site with no vital structure at risk, so it is the benign-non-dangerous exception in this list. The other four options (ureteric, oesophageal, cardiac and pituitary tumours) are all dangerous by virtue of their site despite being histologically benign. Lipoma's danger, unlike theirs, does not come from location.

questions.learning_objective: Exception among benign-dangerous tumours

questions.title: Yellowish, greasy subcutaneous mass
questions.question: A male patient has a subcutaneous mass, soft in consistency. Cut section is yellowish and greasy. What is the diagnosis?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Adenoma is a benign glandular epithelial tumour, not the fatty, yellowish, greasy-cut-section lesion described.
explanations.B: Correct. A soft subcutaneous mass with a yellowish, greasy cut section is the classic gross description of a lipoma, the benign tumour of mature fat cells (adipocytes). The greasy appearance reflects the lipid content of the constituent fat cells, and the soft consistency reflects the lobulated, encapsulated fatty tissue architecture. This gross picture, together with the subcutaneous location, is diagnostic for lipoma among the listed options.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Leiomyoma is a benign smooth-muscle tumour with a firm, whorled cut surface, not a soft, yellowish, greasy one.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Papilloma is a benign tumour of protective epithelium with a papillary (frond-like) architecture, not a fatty, greasy subcutaneous mass.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Osteosarcoma is a malignant bone-forming tumour, inconsistent with this soft, benign-appearing subcutaneous lesion.

questions.learning_objective: Yellowish, greasy subcutaneous mass

questions.title: Uterine submucous mass with whorled cut section
questions.question: A 25-year-old female has a uterine submucous, well-circumscribed mass. Cut section showed whorls. What is the diagnosis?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Adenocarcinoma is a malignant glandular tumour, inconsistent with this well-circumscribed, benign-appearing mass.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Lipoma has a soft, yellow, greasy cut section, not the firm whorled pattern described here.
explanations.C: Correct. A well-circumscribed uterine mass with a whorled cut section is the classic gross appearance of leiomyoma (uterine fibroid), the benign tumour of uterine smooth muscle, whose interlacing bundles of smooth-muscle fascicles produce the whorled pattern on cut section. Its well-circumscribed, pseudocapsulated border is typical of a benign lesion. This is the most common benign uterine tumour and the expected diagnosis for this vignette.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Leiomyosarcoma, the malignant counterpart, would typically show a less well-circumscribed margin, necrosis, haemorrhage or mitotic activity, none of which is described here.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Schwannoma is a benign nerve-sheath tumour, not the smooth-muscle uterine lesion described.

questions.learning_objective: Uterine submucous mass with whorled cut section

questions.title: Cervical lymph node draining tonsillitis
questions.question: An enlarged cervical lymph node draining non-specific tonsillitis represents one of the following processes:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Compensatory hyperplasia follows loss of tissue mass (e.g. bone marrow after haemorrhage), not local infection draining to a node.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Hormonal hyperplasia is driven by a hormone (e.g. breast glandular hyperplasia in pregnancy), not by local infection.
explanations.C: Correct. A cervical lymph node that enlarges while draining a site of local infection, such as non-specific tonsillitis, is undergoing irritation (reactive) hyperplasia — antigenic stimulation expands the node's lymphoid follicles and germinal centres. This is a benign, self-limiting response to the draining infection, not a hormone- or mass-loss-driven process. It resolves as the underlying tonsillitis is treated.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Metaplasia is a change of one differentiated cell type into another, not an increase in lymphoid cellularity.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Neoplasia is autonomous, uncontrolled new growth, not the reactive, self-limiting response to infection described here.

questions.learning_objective: Cervical lymph node draining tonsillitis

questions.title: Myositis ossificans as metaplasia
questions.question: Myositis ossificans is an example of:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Chondrogenic metaplasia would describe formation of cartilage rather than bone; myositis ossificans specifically forms bone within muscle.
explanations.B: Correct. Myositis ossificans is bone formation within skeletal muscle, typically after intramuscular haemorrhage or trauma, and is classified as connective-tissue (mesenchymal) metaplasia, the category covering metaplastic formation of cartilage, bone or fat where these tissues do not normally occur. It is not an epithelial change, so it sits apart from the squamous/columnar metaplasia examples usually discussed. The mesenchymal precursor cells within the muscle differentiate into osteoblasts under the injury stimulus.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Epithelial metaplasia describes a change between epithelial cell types (e.g. columnar to squamous), not the mesenchymal bone-forming process seen in myositis ossificans.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Haematopoeitic metaplasia describes ectopic blood-cell-forming tissue, not the bone formation seen here.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Serosal metaplasia is not the mechanism at work in intramuscular bone formation.

questions.learning_objective: Myositis ossificans as metaplasia

questions.title: Left ventricular response to aortic valve stenosis
questions.question: In case of aortic valve stenosis, the left ventricle is affected by:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Cardiomyocytes are permanent, post-mitotic cells and cannot mount a hyperplastic (cell-number-increasing) response.
explanations.B: Incorrect. "Compensatory" hypertrophy specifically describes enlargement after loss of a paired organ or tissue mass; the aortic-stenosis response is better termed adaptive (pressure-overload) hypertrophy.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Hyperplasia of any kind is not possible in cardiomyocytes, which are permanent cells.
explanations.D: Correct. Aortic valve stenosis imposes a sustained pressure overload on the left ventricle, which responds by adaptive hypertrophy: existing myocytes enlarge (adding sarcomeres) to generate greater contractile force against the raised afterload, increasing wall thickness. Because cardiomyocytes are permanent cells, this enlargement of existing cells, rather than an increase in their number, is the only way the ventricle can adapt. This is the same pressure-overload hypertrophy mechanism seen in chronic uncontrolled hypertension.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Atrophy is a decrease in cell/tissue size, the opposite of the expected pressure-overload response.

questions.learning_objective: Left ventricular response to aortic valve stenosis

questions.title: Cervical lymph node response to acute tonsillitis, child
questions.question: A 4-year-old female presents with difficulty swallowing; throat examination shows acute tonsillitis. Her cervical lymph nodes will show a picture of:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Compensatory hyperplasia follows loss of tissue mass, not local infection draining to a node.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Lymph node cells do not respond to infection by hypertrophy; they respond by an increase in cell numbers (hyperplasia).
explanations.C: Correct. As with any lymph node draining a site of acute local infection, the cervical nodes draining this child's acute tonsillitis undergo irritative (reactive) hyperplasia — antigenic stimulation expands lymphoid follicles and increases lymphocyte and macrophage numbers. This is the same fact tested by the adult tonsillitis-draining-node vignette elsewhere in this exam, applied here to a paediatric case. It is a benign, self-limiting reactive process.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Adaptive hypertrophy describes an enlargement response to a mechanical/functional load (e.g. cardiac pressure overload), not a lymph node's response to infection.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Metaplasia is a change of differentiated cell type, not the lymphoid hyperplastic response to infection described here.

questions.title: Benign tumour of protective epithelium
questions.question: A benign tumour of protective epithelium is one of the followings:

explanations.A: Correct. Papilloma is the benign tumour arising from protective epithelium (stratified squamous or transitional epithelium), growing as finger-like fronds covered by that same epithelium. This distinguishes it from the benign glandular epithelial tumours (adenoma, cystadenoma) and from the benign mesenchymal tumours (chondroma, lipoma) also listed. Naming the tumour by its epithelial type of origin (protective versus glandular) is the key classification principle being tested.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Adenoma is the benign tumour of glandular (secretory), not protective, epithelium.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Cystadenoma is a cystic variant of adenoma, still arising from glandular epithelium, not protective epithelium.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Chondroma is a benign tumour of cartilage, a mesenchymal tissue, not an epithelial tumour at all.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Lipoma is a benign tumour of fat, a mesenchymal tissue, not an epithelial tumour.

questions.learning_objective: Benign tumour of protective epithelium

questions.title: Signet ring morphology in a benign tumour
questions.question: Signet ring microscopic morphology presents in the following tumour:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Leiomyoma cells are spindle-shaped smooth-muscle cells, not signet-ring-shaped.
explanations.B: Correct. In lipoma, a mature fat cell (adipocyte) is filled by a single large lipid vacuole that compresses and flattens the nucleus against the cell membrane, producing a signet-ring appearance on histology — the lipid-filled counterpart to the mucin-filled signet ring cell of gastric carcinoma. This is simply the normal, benign morphology of mature adipose tissue, not a sign of malignancy in this context. Recognising this appearance as fat-filled (rather than the malignant mucin-filled pattern) depends on the tissue context.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Adenoma cells retain a glandular architecture and do not characteristically show a signet-ring appearance.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Chondroma is composed of mature cartilage cells (chondrocytes) within a cartilaginous matrix, not signet-ring cells.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Osteoma is composed of mature bone, not signet-ring cells.

questions.learning_objective: Signet ring morphology in a benign tumour

questions.title: Benign tumour causing infertility
questions.question: One of the following benign tumours could be a cause of infertility:

explanations.A: Incorrect. A lipoma in its typical subcutaneous site has no relationship to the reproductive tract or fertility.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A generic adenoma is not specifically implicated in infertility the way a uterine leiomyoma is.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A papilloma of protective epithelium is not a recognised cause of infertility.
explanations.D: Correct. Leiomyoma (uterine fibroid), especially a submucous leiomyoma distorting the endometrial cavity, is a well-recognised benign cause of infertility, by mechanically interfering with implantation, distorting the cavity or obstructing the tubal ostia. Its site within the uterine wall relative to the cavity determines its impact on fertility. Among the benign tumours listed, only leiomyoma has this direct anatomical relationship to the reproductive tract.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Fibroadenoma is a benign breast tumour and has no direct relationship to uterine fertility.

questions.learning_objective: Benign tumour causing infertility

questions.title: Characteristic growth pattern of benign tumours
questions.question: Benign tumours are characterized by:

explanations.A: Correct. Benign tumours are characterised by a slow rate of growth, reflecting their generally low mitotic activity and lack of the aggressive proliferative drive of malignant tumours. This slow growth typically allows the surrounding tissue time to form a fibrous capsule around the lesion, contributing to its well-circumscribed appearance. Slow growth, expansile (non-infiltrative) behaviour, and well-defined margins together define the benign growth pattern.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Rapid growth is a feature of malignant, not benign, tumours.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Infiltrative growth into surrounding tissue is a malignant feature; benign tumours grow by pushing/expansion, remaining well-circumscribed.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Common recurrence after excision is more typical of some malignant or locally aggressive lesions, not the general rule for benign tumours, which usually do not recur once completely excised.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Ill-defined margins describe the infiltrative edge of a malignant tumour, not the well-defined margin typical of a benign one.

questions.learning_objective: Characteristic growth pattern of benign tumours

questions.title: Characteristic feature of malignant tumours
questions.question: Malignant tumours are characterized by:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Capsulation is a benign feature; malignant tumours lack a true capsule because they infiltrate surrounding tissue.
explanations.B: Correct. Malignant tumours characteristically become fixed to surrounding tissue as they infiltrate through normal tissue planes rather than pushing them aside, unlike a benign tumour's well-circumscribed, mobile growth pattern. This fixation is a key clinical sign on examination (a fixed, immobile mass) and reflects the underlying infiltrative biology. It is one of the paired gross criteria, alongside rapid growth, hard consistency and everted ulcer edges, that distinguish malignant from benign tumours.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Malignant tumours can reach a large size given their rapid growth; small size is not a defining malignant feature.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Malignant tumours typically show numerous, often abnormal mitotic figures, not few.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Malignant tumours typically show pleomorphic (varied), not uniform, nuclei.

questions.learning_objective: Characteristic feature of malignant tumours

questions.title: Route of spread of locally malignant tumours
questions.question: Route of spread of locally malignant tumours is:

explanations.A: Correct. A locally malignant tumour, such as basal cell carcinoma, is by definition capable only of local (infiltrative) spread into adjacent tissue; it lacks the capacity for distant metastasis by any route. This is exactly what distinguishes "locally malignant" as an intermediate category from a fully malignant tumour capable of metastasizing. Its behaviour is locally destructive but not systemically dangerous.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Blood spread is a distant-metastasis route that a locally malignant tumour, by definition, does not use.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Lymphatic embolization carries tumour emboli to distant/regional nodes, a capability a purely locally malignant tumour lacks.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Transcoelomic spread seeds a body cavity at a distance, which a locally malignant tumour does not do.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Lymphatic permeation, while a form of spread along a channel, still represents a route toward regional/distant disease, beyond the local-only behaviour that defines a locally malignant tumour.

questions.learning_objective: Route of spread of locally malignant tumours

questions.title: Feature distinguishing sarcoma from carcinoma
questions.question: All the following are features of sarcoma except:

explanations.A: Incorrect (this IS a true sarcoma feature, not the exception). Sarcomas classically spread haematogenously (blood spread).
explanations.B: Incorrect (true sarcoma feature). Sarcomas are typically very rapidly growing tumours.
explanations.C: Correct. Unlike carcinoma, which arises from epithelium and typically passes through a recognised in-situ (pre-invasive) phase before invading, sarcoma arises directly from mesenchymal tissue and has no equivalent in-situ phase — it is invasive from the outset. "Presence of an in situ component" is therefore the false statement (the exception) among the listed sarcoma features. The other four options (blood spread, rapid growth, fleshy consistency, high-grade anaplasia) are all true, recognised features of sarcoma.
explanations.D: Incorrect (true sarcoma feature). Sarcomas classically have a soft, fleshy cut-surface consistency.
explanations.E: Incorrect (true sarcoma feature). Sarcomas frequently show a high grade of anaplasia (poor differentiation).

questions.learning_objective: Feature distinguishing sarcoma from carcinoma

questions.title: Benign non-dangerous tumour
questions.question: One of the following tumours is a benign non-dangerous tumour:

explanations.A: Incorrect (this IS benign-dangerous). A cardiac myxoma can obstruct a valve orifice despite being histologically benign.
explanations.B: Incorrect (benign-dangerous). A cardiac rhabdomyoma can obstruct the outflow tract or cause arrhythmia despite benign histology.
explanations.C: Incorrect (benign-dangerous). A benign oesophageal tumour can obstruct the narrow oesophageal lumen.
explanations.D: Correct. A forearm lipoma sits in an accommodating subcutaneous site with no vital structure at risk, making it benign-non-dangerous — harmless histology in a harmless location. This contrasts directly with the other four options, all of which are benign tumours rendered dangerous purely by their site (heart, oesophagus, pituitary). Site, not histology, is what separates the benign-dangerous category from the benign-non-dangerous one.
explanations.E: Incorrect (benign-dangerous). A pituitary adenoma causes mass effect and hormonal disturbance despite benign histology.

questions.learning_objective: Benign non-dangerous tumour

questions.title: Autopsy finding in a trained marathon runner
questions.question: A 35-year-old marathon runner died in a motor vehicle accident while driving to work. At autopsy, which of the following features could be identified through gross and microscopic examination of the organs?

options.E: Pathologic hyperplasia of the skeletal muscle

explanations.A: Incorrect. A trained runner's skeletal muscle is expected to be hypertrophied (from training), not atrophied.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The runner's cardiac change from training is physiologic, not pathologic, and cardiomyocytes cannot undergo hyperplasia.
explanations.C: Correct. Sustained endurance training drives physiologic hypertrophy of the heart — an adaptive, reversible enlargement of cardiomyocytes in response to the normal physiological demand of regular exercise, distinct from the pathologic hypertrophy seen in chronic hypertension or valve disease. This is the expected, benign autopsy finding in a trained athlete's heart and should not be mistaken for occult cardiac disease. The same physiologic-adaptation principle also explains the runner's hypertrophied (not atrophied) skeletal muscle.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Cardiomyocytes are permanent, post-mitotic cells and cannot undergo hyperplasia; the training-induced change is hypertrophy.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The skeletal muscle change from training is physiologic hypertrophy (larger fibres), not pathologic hyperplasia.

questions.learning_objective: Autopsy finding in a trained marathon runner

questions.title: Atrophy in poliomyelitis
questions.question: Which type of atrophy occurs in poliomyelitis patients?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Aging (senescence) atrophy is a generalized, age-related process, not the specific mechanism in poliomyelitis.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Disuse atrophy occurs with immobilisation of a muscle whose nerve supply is intact, which is not the mechanism in poliomyelitis.
explanations.C: Correct. Poliovirus destroys anterior horn motor neurons in the spinal cord; the skeletal muscle fibres innervated by those neurons then lose their nerve supply and undergo neuropathic (denervation) atrophy. This is distinct from disuse atrophy, in which the nerve supply remains intact. Neuropathic atrophy is one of the five recognised patterns of localized pathological atrophy (alongside disuse, pressure, vascular and hormonal).
explanations.D: Incorrect. Senescence atrophy is the same as aging atrophy, a generalized process, not specific to poliomyelitis's mechanism.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Vascular atrophy follows reduced blood supply (ischaemia), not motor neuron destruction as in poliomyelitis.

questions.learning_objective: Atrophy in poliomyelitis

questions.title: Route of spread of locally malignant tumours (characterisation)
questions.question: Locally malignant tumours are characterized by:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Distant spread is exactly what a locally malignant tumour, by definition, cannot do.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Homing is a step of distant metastatic colonisation, not a feature of a purely locally malignant tumour.
explanations.C: Correct. Locally malignant tumours are characterised by local (infiltrative) spread only, without the capacity to metastasize distantly. Basal cell carcinoma is the classic example: it can invade and destroy local tissue extensively but essentially never spreads to lymph nodes or distant organs. This local-only spread is the defining behavioural feature that separates this category from a fully malignant, metastasis-capable tumour.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Rapid growth rate is a feature more typical of fully malignant tumours generally, not the specific defining feature of the "locally malignant" category, which is about the extent of spread rather than growth speed.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Vascular dissemination is a distant-spread route, which a locally malignant tumour does not use.

questions.title: Exception among routes of distant spread
questions.question: The following are examples of distant spread except:

explanations.A: Incorrect (true distant-spread route). Blood (haematogenous) spread carries tumour cells to distant organs.
explanations.B: Incorrect (true distant-spread route). Implantation (surgical seeding) transfers tumour cells to a new site at operation.
explanations.C: Incorrect (true distant-spread route). Lymphatic embolism carries detached tumour emboli to regional or distant nodes.
explanations.D: Incorrect (true distant-spread route). Transcoelomic spread seeds a body cavity lined by serous membrane at a distance from the primary.
explanations.E: Correct. Ulceration of a tumour through overlying skin or mucosa is a local complication of a tumour's growth — the tumour outgrowing its blood supply and breaking down the surface — not itself a mechanism of distant spread. It does not carry tumour cells to a new site the way blood, lymphatic, transcoelomic or implantation spread do. It is therefore the correct exception among these five listed processes.

questions.learning_objective: Exception among routes of distant spread

questions.title: Tumour depth and prognosis
questions.question: Tumour with poor prognosis is:

explanations.A: Correct. A deeply located tumour tends to be diagnosed later, is harder to resect completely, and lies closer to more anatomical routes for local and distant spread, giving it a worse prognosis than an equivalent superficial tumour. Depth of location is therefore an independent adverse prognostic factor, alongside grade, stage, site and histological type. This is the opposite situation to the other listed options, all of which describe favourable prognostic features.
explanations.B: Incorrect. An early-staged tumour has a better, not worse, prognosis.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A superficial tumour is more easily detected and resected, giving a better prognosis than a deep one.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Having already undergone therapy is not itself a marker of poor prognosis; it describes treatment status, not tumour biology.
explanations.E: Incorrect. A well-differentiated tumour has a better, not worse, prognosis than a poorly differentiated one.

questions.learning_objective: Tumour depth and prognosis

questions.title: False statement about a colonic adenomatous polyp
questions.question: A 50-year-old male complains of bleeding per rectum. Biopsy revealed proliferated glands with a mild degree of atypia, with no necrosis or haemorrhage; diagnosis: adenoma of the colon. One of the following criteria regarding this tumour is wrong:

explanations.A: Incorrect (this is a true statement, not the exception). A colonic adenoma is indeed precancerous, carrying malignant potential via the adenoma-carcinoma sequence.
explanations.B: Correct. Describing a colonic adenoma as "not precancerous" is false — its defining clinical significance is precisely its precancerous potential, which is why it warrants colonoscopic removal and surveillance. This is the wrong statement among the five listed. The other four statements (precancerous, may be single, may be multiple, may occur in any part of the colon) are all true of colonic adenomatous polyps.
explanations.C: Incorrect (true statement). A colonic adenoma can present as a single lesion.
explanations.D: Incorrect (true statement). Colonic adenomas can also be multiple (synchronous).
explanations.E: Incorrect (true statement). A colonic adenoma can arise in any segment of the colon.

questions.title: Krukenberg tumour's route of spread
questions.question: Krukenberg's tumour is an example of one of the following:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Krukenberg tumour is classically taught as an example of transcoelomic (peritoneal) spread rather than haematogenous spread.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The ovaries are not directly contiguous with the usual gastric or colonic primary, so this is not direct spread.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Krukenberg tumour is classically attributed to transcoelomic, not lymphatic, spread.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A Krukenberg tumour is by definition a metastatic, not a primary, ovarian tumour.
explanations.E: Correct. A Krukenberg tumour — bilateral ovarian metastases, classically from a gastric or colonic (signet-ring) carcinoma — is taught as an example of transcoelomic spread, in which tumour cells shed from the primary seed the peritoneal cavity and implant on the ovarian surfaces. This is the standard teaching link between Krukenberg tumour and one of the five named routes of malignant spread. Recognising it reinforces that not every ovarian mass is a primary ovarian neoplasm.

questions.title: Breast glandular epithelial response to prolactin in pregnancy
questions.question: During the third trimester of pregnancy, prolactin secretion from the pituitary gland stimulates glandular epithelial cells of the breast to produce milk. The glandular epithelial cells typically respond by undergoing:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Atrophy is a decrease in cell size/number, the opposite of the proliferative response needed for milk production.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Dysplasia is a disordered, potentially premalignant change, not the normal physiological response to prolactin.
explanations.C: Correct. Rising prolactin in the third trimester drives hormonal hyperplasia of breast glandular epithelial cells — an increase in secretory cell numbers — enabling the gland to produce milk. Because these glandular cells retain proliferative capacity, a hormonal stimulus increases their number (hyperplasia) rather than only their size. This is a fully physiological, reversible change that regresses after weaning.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Hypertrophy (increase in cell size without division) is the response of a permanent, non-dividing cell (like cardiomyocytes) to a stimulus, not the expected response of proliferation-capable glandular epithelium.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Metaplasia is a change of cell type, not the expected physiological response to prolactin in pregnancy.

questions.title: Histologic diagnosis of a prolactin-secreting pituitary tumour
questions.question: A 35-year-old female complains of nipple discharge and irregular menses of 5 months' duration. Physical examination reveals a milky discharge from both nipples. MRI shows an enlargement of the anterior pituitary. Which of the following is the most likely histologic diagnosis of this patient's pituitary tumour?

explanations.A: Correct. This presentation — bilateral galactorrhoea and menstrual irregularity from hyperprolactinaemia, with an MRI-confirmed anterior pituitary mass — is the classic prolactinoma picture. A prolactinoma is histologically an adenoma: a discrete, benign, autonomously secreting neoplasm, distinguished from a diffuse, non-neoplastic gland enlargement (hyperplasia). Its autonomous prolactin secretion suppresses gonadotropin-releasing hormone pulsatility (causing the menstrual irregularity) while acting directly on breast tissue (causing galactorrhoea).
explanations.B: Incorrect. Hamartoma is a disorganised overgrowth of tissue native to the site, not the discrete secretory neoplasm described here.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Hyperplasia would be a diffuse gland enlargement, not the discrete mass an MRI-confirmed pituitary tumour implies.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Papilloma is a benign tumour of protective epithelium, not the pituitary endocrine cell type involved here.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Teratoma contains tissue from multiple germ layers and is not the expected histology for a functioning pituitary mass presenting this way.

questions.title: Best description of neoplasia
questions.question: Which one of the following best describes neoplasia?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Neoplastic cells are frequently abnormal in shape (pleomorphic), not normal.
explanations.B: Correct. Neoplasia is defined as new growth that is autonomous — independent of the normal stimulus that provoked it and independent of the controls that would normally limit growth. This autonomy is what makes neoplastic growth continue (and, once established, be irreversible) even after any inciting factor is removed, unlike a reversible adaptive change. It is the single feature that most precisely captures what distinguishes neoplasia from a reactive or adaptive growth response.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Neoplasia, especially malignant neoplasia, characteristically has a significant, not limited, effect on the host.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Neoplastic tissue typically shows a disordered, not normal, cellular/architectural pattern.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Neoplastic growth is purposeless to the host, not usefully functional.

questions.title: Histology of a neck lipoma
questions.question: A 25-year-old male presented with a well-circumscribed mass at the back of the neck. The excised mass is lobulated and its cut section displayed bulging, greasy, pale-yellow tissue. The microscopic picture of this lesion reveals lobules of:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Bone would appear as mineralised trabeculae, not the bulging, greasy, pale-yellow lobulated tissue described.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Cartilage has a firm, glistening, bluish-white cut surface, not a greasy, pale-yellow one.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Endothelial cells line vascular channels (as in a haemangioma), which would not present as bulging, greasy, yellow lobules.
explanations.D: Correct. A well-circumscribed, lobulated mass with a bulging, greasy, pale-yellow cut section is the classic gross description of a lipoma, and its microscopic picture confirms this: lobules of mature fat cells (adipocytes) separated by thin fibrous septa. The greasy, yellow appearance directly reflects the lipid content of these fat cells. This gross-and-microscopic combination is diagnostic for lipoma.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Muscle fibres have a red-brown, striated gross appearance, not the greasy yellow appearance described.

questions.title: Left ventricular finding in uncontrolled hypertension
questions.question: A 55-year-old female has suffered from hypertension for 10 years. She is on antihypertensive drugs, but her blood pressure remains uncontrolled. Which of the following is an expected finding in her left ventricle?

explanations.A: Correct. Ten years of uncontrolled hypertension imposes sustained pressure overload on the left ventricle, which responds with adaptive hypertrophy — myocyte enlargement that increases wall thickness and contractile force to cope with the raised afterload, the same pathologic-pressure-overload response seen with aortic stenosis. Because cardiomyocytes are permanent cells, this is enlargement of existing cells, not an increase in cell number. Persisting uncontrolled hypertension is exactly the chronic stimulus that drives this adaptation.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Aging atrophy is an unrelated, generalized age-related process, not the specific pressure-overload response expected here.
explanations.C: Incorrect. "Compensatory" hypertrophy specifically follows loss of a paired organ/tissue mass, not sustained pressure overload; the correct term here is adaptive hypertrophy.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Hormonal hyperplasia describes a hormone-driven increase in cell number in a proliferation-capable tissue (e.g. breast), not the cardiomyocyte hypertrophic response to pressure overload.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Physiological hypertrophy describes the reversible, exercise-driven cardiac adaptation of a trained athlete, not the pathologic adaptation to chronic uncontrolled hypertension.

questions.learning_objective: Left ventricular finding in uncontrolled hypertension

questions.title: Hyperplasia of lymphoid tissue after antigenic stimulation
questions.question: Which type of hyperplasia occurs in lymphoid tissue after antigenic stimulation?

explanations.A: Incorrect. "Aging" describes a physiological atrophy pattern, not the hyperplastic response to antigenic stimulation.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Compensatory hyperplasia responds to loss of tissue mass, not to antigenic stimulation.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Hormonal hyperplasia is driven by a hormone, not by antigenic (immune) stimulation.
explanations.D: Correct. Antigenic stimulation of lymphoid tissue — the response to a local infection or chronic irritation draining to that tissue — produces irritation (reactive) hyperplasia, with expansion of lymphoid follicles and germinal centres. This is the same fact as the cervical-lymph-node-draining-tonsillitis vignettes tested elsewhere in this exam, phrased here as the general underlying category. It is a benign, self-limiting immune response.
explanations.E: Incorrect. "Physiological" hyperplasia is a broader category (including hormonal hyperplasia); the specific type driven by antigenic/infective stimulation is irritation hyperplasia.

questions.learning_objective: Hyperplasia of lymphoid tissue after antigenic stimulation

questions.title: Growth disturbance in cachexia
questions.question: Which of the following growth disturbances is most likely to occur in patients suffering from cachexia?

explanations.A: Correct. Cachexia is a generalized (systemic) wasting state, driven by malignancy, chronic infection, malnutrition or chronic organ failure, that produces generalized atrophy of skeletal muscle and fat throughout the body. This is distinct from the five localized pathological atrophy patterns (disuse, pressure, vascular, neuropathic, hormonal), which affect only one region or tissue. Recognising atrophy as the expected finding in cachexia prompts a search for the underlying systemic driver.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Dysplasia is disordered, potentially premalignant epithelial growth, not the wasting change seen in cachexia.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Hyperplasia is an increase in cell number, the opposite of the wasting seen in cachexia.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Hypertrophy is an increase in cell size, the opposite of the wasting seen in cachexia.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Metaplasia is a change of cell type, not the generalized wasting change of cachexia.

questions.learning_objective: Growth disturbance in cachexia

questions.title: False statement about rodent ulcer
questions.question: All the following are true about rodent ulcer of the face except:

options.A: Edges of the ulcer are raised everted edges
options.D: Microscopic picture of basal cell carcinoma

explanations.A: Correct. Rodent ulcer (basal cell carcinoma) classically has raised, rolled (pearly, rolled) edges, not everted edges — "everted edges" is the false statement here, and is instead the classic description of a different pattern of malignant ulcer. The other four statements (locally malignant, basosquamous transformation potential, basal cell carcinoma microscopy, local spread) are all true features of rodent ulcer.
explanations.B: Incorrect (true statement). Basal cell carcinoma is locally malignant — locally destructive but essentially never metastasizing.
explanations.C: Incorrect (true statement). Basal cell carcinoma can transform into the more aggressive basosquamous carcinoma.
explanations.D: Incorrect (true statement). Microscopically, a rodent ulcer shows the features of basal cell carcinoma by definition.
explanations.E: Incorrect (true statement). A rodent ulcer spreads locally, consistent with its locally malignant behaviour.

questions.title: Definition of transcoelomic spread
questions.question: Which of the following best describes transcoelomic spread?

options.A: Detached malignant cell spread through luminal organs
options.D: Occurs in tumors of organs covered by serous membranes

explanations.A: Incorrect. Transcoelomic spread involves a body cavity lined by serous membrane, not a luminal (hollow-organ) route.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Transcoelomic spread is a route of distant (within-cavity) spread, not local spread confined to adjacent tissue.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Transcoelomic spread is a route used by fully malignant tumours capable of distant spread, not a feature specific to locally malignant tumours (which by definition do not spread distantly).
explanations.D: Correct. Transcoelomic spread occurs in tumours of organs covered by serous membranes (peritoneum, pleura, pericardium): detached malignant cells shed from the tumour surface and seed elsewhere within the same body cavity, as in ovarian carcinoma seeding the peritoneal cavity or a Krukenberg tumour from gastric carcinoma. This is one of the five recognised routes of malignant spread. It depends specifically on the primary organ being covered by a serous membrane, unlike organs lacking such a covering.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Spread during surgical operations describes implantation, a distinct route from transcoelomic spread.

questions.learning_objective: Definition of transcoelomic spread

questions.title: Best description of Krukenberg tumour
questions.question: Which of the following best describes Krukenberg tumour?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Krukenberg tumour is fully malignant and metastatic, not merely locally malignant.
explanations.B: Correct. A Krukenberg tumour is, by definition, a metastatic ovarian tumour — most classically from a gastric (signet-ring) or colonic primary — rather than a tumour that originates in the ovary itself. Recognising this prevents mistaking bilateral ovarian masses for primary ovarian neoplasms and prompts a search for the (often occult) gastrointestinal primary. Its classic spread mechanism to the ovaries is transcoelomic seeding of the peritoneal cavity.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A Krukenberg tumour is specifically the opposite of a primary ovarian tumour — it is a metastasis to the ovary from elsewhere.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Krukenberg tumour is classically attributed to transcoelomic, not haematogenous, spread.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Krukenberg tumour is classically attributed to transcoelomic, not lymphatic, spread.

questions.title: Bladder biopsy: full-thickness atypia, intact basement membrane
questions.question: A 62-year-old man complains of pain on urination. Cystoscopy revealed a red area on the bladder mucosa that was biopsied and showed cells with marked hyperchromatism and increased nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio, involving the full thickness of the epithelium, confined to the epithelium above an intact basement membrane. Which of the following terms best describes these biopsy findings?

explanations.A: Correct. Full-thickness epithelial atypia (marked hyperchromatism, increased nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio, disturbed polarity throughout the epithelium) with the basement membrane still intact and no invasion beneath it is the defining picture of carcinoma in situ — a pre-invasive stage of carcinoma. This distinguishes it from both a lesser degree of atypia (dysplasia, which does not involve the full epithelial thickness) and frankly invasive carcinoma (which by definition breaches the basement membrane). The intact basement membrane is the single most important finding separating this diagnosis from invasive carcinoma.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Hyperplasia describes an increase in normal-appearing cell numbers, not the marked cytological atypia described here.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Invasive carcinoma requires breach of the basement membrane, which is explicitly described as intact here.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Metaplasia describes a change of differentiated cell type, not the atypical, hyperchromatic epithelium described.
explanations.E: Incorrect. "Minimal" dysplasia understates the severity described; full-thickness atypia is carcinoma in situ, a more advanced pre-invasive change than minimal dysplasia.

questions.title: Neoplasm most likely to arise from viral oncogenesis
questions.question: Some neoplasms appear to develop from viral oncogenesis. Which of the following neoplasms is most likely to arise in this manner?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Breast cancer does not have an established, defining viral-oncogenesis mechanism.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Prostate cancer does not have an established, defining viral-oncogenesis mechanism.
explanations.C: Correct. Carcinoma of the cervix is the neoplasm most classically and mechanistically linked to viral oncogenesis, driven by human papillomavirus (HPV). High-risk HPV's E6 and E7 oncoproteins respectively degrade p53 and inactivate Rb, disabling two central tumour-suppressor checkpoints in cervical epithelial cells and driving progression from dysplasia to invasive carcinoma. This well-defined mechanism underlies both HPV vaccination (primary prevention) and cervical screening (secondary prevention).
explanations.D: Incorrect. Ovarian cancer does not have an established, defining viral-oncogenesis mechanism.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Retinoblastoma's mechanism is inherited or somatic loss of the RB1 tumour-suppressor gene, not a viral mechanism.

questions.title: Exception among examples of metaplasia
questions.question: Which of the following conditions is not an example of metaplasia?

explanations.A: Incorrect (this IS a true metaplasia example). Adenoacanthoma shows squamous metaplasia within an adenocarcinoma.
explanations.B: Incorrect (true metaplasia example). Barrett's oesophagus is squamous-to-intestinal (columnar) metaplasia of the distal oesophagus.
explanations.C: Correct. Congenital pyloric stenosis is a congenital condition of pyloric smooth-muscle hypertrophy causing gastric outlet obstruction; it involves more muscle of the already-correct cell type, not a substitution of one differentiated cell type for another. It is therefore not an example of metaplasia, unlike the other four true metaplasia examples listed. Recognising this distinguishes hypertrophy (more of the same cell type) from metaplasia (a genuine change of cell type).
explanations.D: Incorrect (true metaplasia example, taught alongside coelomic-metaplasia theories of pathogenesis). Endometriosis is grouped with metaplasia examples in this curriculum.

questions.title: Category of a pituitary adenoma
questions.question: A 24-year-old female complains of headache and blurring of vision. Radiological examination revealed a pituitary tumour. Biopsy showed adenoma. Which category does this tumour belong to?

explanations.A: Correct. A pituitary adenoma is histologically benign, yet dangerous by virtue of its site: it produces headache and visual disturbance through mass effect on the optic chiasm, exactly as this patient presents. It belongs, alongside cardiac, oesophageal and ureteric benign tumours, to the benign-dangerous category, where danger comes from location rather than malignant histology.

explanations.C: Incorrect. "Locally malignant" describes a tumour with some infiltrative malignant behaviour (e.g. basal cell carcinoma), not a benign adenoma.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The biopsy explicitly shows adenoma, a benign diagnosis, not a malignant epithelial tumour.

questions.title: False statement about general criteria of neoplasm
questions.question: Regarding general criteria of neoplasm, one of the followings is wrong:

explanations.A: Incorrect (true criterion). Autonomy — independence from the normal controlling stimulus — is a true defining feature of neoplasia.
explanations.B: Incorrect (true criterion). Neoplastic growth is purposeless to the host.
explanations.C: Correct. This irreversibility, alongside autonomy, is one of the features that most sharply separates neoplasia from an adaptive growth response.

questions.title: Role of matrix metalloproteases in tumour spread
questions.question: Matrix metalloproteases are concerned in one of the following steps of spread of malignant tumours:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Cell-cell detachment is mediated by loss of adhesion molecules (e.g. E-cadherin), not by matrix metalloproteases.
explanations.B: Correct. Matrix metalloproteases (MMPs) are the enzymes responsible for degrading the extracellular matrix and basement membrane, clearing a path for the tumour cell to migrate through — the step immediately after cell-cell detachment in the local invasion cascade. This enzymatic degradation is what allows a tumour cell to physically breach the basement membrane and invade into surrounding stroma. Without MMP-mediated matrix degradation, a detached tumour cell could not progress to migration or eventual intravasation.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Homing (localising at a distant site) is a late metastatic step, not the specific role of matrix metalloproteases within the local invasion cascade.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Intravasation (entry into a vessel) follows matrix degradation and migration; it is not itself the MMP-mediated step.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Migration is the step after matrix degradation has cleared a path, not the enzymatic degradation step itself.

questions.learning_objective: Role of matrix metalloproteases in tumour spread

questions.title: Factor not favouring circulating tumour cell survival
questions.question: Dissemination of tumour cells through vascular channels: one of the following does not favor tumour cell survival:

options.A: Aggregate with other blood cells particularly platelets
options.C: Tumor cells aggregate to form clumps
options.D: Tumor cells are covered by blood components

explanations.A: Incorrect (this DOES favour survival). Platelet aggregation around a circulating tumour cell shields it from immune attack.
explanations.B: Correct. A functioning host innate and adaptive immune response actively seeks out and destroys circulating tumour cells, reducing rather than favouring their survival in the bloodstream — the opposite effect from the other listed factors, which all shield the tumour cell from that same immune attack. This is why immunosuppression is associated with higher rates of metastatic spread. Recognising this item as asking for the factor that hinders (not helps) survival is the key to answering it correctly.
explanations.C: Incorrect (this DOES favour survival). Tumour-cell clumping helps shield cells within the clump from immune destruction.
explanations.D: Incorrect (this DOES favour survival). A coating of blood components physically shields the tumour cell from immune recognition.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Option B (innate and adaptive immune defences) is the one factor that does not favour tumour cell survival, so "none of the above" is not correct.

questions.title: Route of spread demonstrated by peau d'orange breast carcinoma
questions.question: A 42-year-old female presented with a breast mass and skin of the breast showing peau d'orange morphology. Enlarged axillary lymph nodes were also identified, and biopsy of an axillary lymph node showed metastatic breast carcinoma. Which route of spread of malignant tumour is demonstrated in this scenario?

explanations.A: Incorrect. There is no evidence of distant blood-borne spread here; the skin change and nodal disease reflect a lymphatic mechanism.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Direct spread alone does not explain the peau d'orange skin change, which specifically reflects lymphatic channel involvement.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Lymphatic embolization refers to detached tumour emboli reaching a node; the skin change described here specifically reflects permeation (growth along the lymphatic channel itself), not embolization.
explanations.D: Correct. Peau d'orange (orange-peel) skin change over a breast carcinoma results from lymphatic permeation — direct tumour growth along the dermal lymphatic channels, which blocks lymphatic drainage and produces cutaneous oedema around the fixed hair follicles, giving the characteristic dimpled appearance. Together with the biopsy-proven axillary nodal metastasis, this demonstrates lymphatic spread specifically by the permeation mechanism. This is a classic clinical sign of locally advanced breast carcinoma.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Transcoelomic spread applies to serosa-covered organs seeding a body cavity, not to breast skin and axillary nodal involvement.

questions.title: Type of thymic atrophy after puberty
questions.question: Atrophy of the thymus after puberty is a type of .............. atrophy:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Disuse atrophy is a pathological, localized pattern (e.g. an immobilised limb), not the normal age-related thymic involution.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Pressure atrophy is a pathological, localized pattern (from a mass or expanding lesion), not the normal thymic process after puberty.
explanations.C: Incorrect. "Senescence" describes generalized age-related change; the thymus's post-pubertal involution is specifically classed here as physiological atrophy rather than the senescence pattern.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Vascular atrophy follows reduced blood supply, not the normal, hormonally-timed thymic involution after puberty.
explanations.E: Correct. The thymus normally undergoes physiological atrophy (involution) after puberty, with progressive replacement of thymic lymphoid tissue by fat, as the adaptive immune repertoire matures and the gland's need for large-scale T-cell education declines. This is a normal, expected, age-timed process, distinct from the pathological atrophy patterns (disuse, pressure, vascular, neuropathic, hormonal). It explains the low thymic mass typically seen incidentally on adult imaging.

questions.question: Which type of metaplasia occurs in urinary bladder Bilharziasis?

options.B: Transformation of columnar epithelium to squamous epithelium
options.C: Transformation of squamous epithelium to intestinal epithelium

questions.title: Cancer associated with aflatoxin
questions.question: Which of the following cancers is associated with aflatoxin carcinogen?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Mesothelioma is classically associated with asbestos exposure, not aflatoxin.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Breast carcinoma does not have an established causal link to aflatoxin exposure.
explanations.C: Correct. Aflatoxin, a mycotoxin produced by Aspergillus flavus contaminating stored grains and nuts, is metabolised to a reactive epoxide that forms DNA adducts in hepatocytes, producing a signature TP53 mutation and driving hepatocellular carcinoma, especially synergistically with chronic hepatitis B infection. This is the classic, well-established chemical-carcinogen link tested here. Recognising it underlies both food-safety measures and hepatitis B-related cancer-risk counselling.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Prostatic carcinoma does not have an established causal link to aflatoxin exposure.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Urothelial carcinoma is classically linked to aromatic amine exposure, not aflatoxin.

questions.title: Bladder biopsy: papillary fronds, no invasion
questions.question: A 35-year-old male complains of hematuria. Radiology revealed a urinary bladder mass. Biopsy showed a tumor composed of thin papillary fronds with a central fibrovascular core, covered by malignant epithelial cells with anaplastic features. There was no invasion. What is your diagnosis?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Inverted papilloma is a benign lesion growing inward (endophytic), not the exophytic papillary fronds with malignant/anaplastic cells described here.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Invasive urothelial carcinoma requires breach of the basement membrane/lamina propria, which is explicitly excluded here ("no invasion").
explanations.C: Correct. Thin papillary fronds with a central fibrovascular core, covered by malignant urothelial cells showing anaplastic features, with no invasion of the underlying tissue, is the defining picture of papillary urothelial carcinoma — a non-invasive bladder tumour that grows exophytically into the lumen along fibrovascular cores rather than invading downward. Malignant cytological features (anaplasia) can coexist with this non-invasive growth pattern. This distinction from invasive urothelial carcinoma (which by definition breaches the basement membrane) is the key point tested here.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Leiomyosarcoma is a mesenchymal malignant tumour, not the epithelial papillary lesion described.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Squamous cell carcinoma is a different histological type, not the papillary urothelial architecture described.

questions.learning_objective: Bladder biopsy: papillary fronds, no invasion

questions.title: Orbital mass in a young child, cambium layer
questions.question: A male child, 3 years old, has progressive exophthalmos. Radiology revealed a large orbital mass. Biopsy revealed sheets of small round blue cells admixed with spindle-shaped cells in a myxoid stroma creating a cambium layer. Occasional strap cells were also identified. What is your diagnosis?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Chondrosarcoma is a cartilage-forming malignant tumour, not the small-round-blue-cell/cambium-layer/strap-cell picture described.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Fibrosarcoma is a fibroblastic spindle-cell tumour without the strap cells or small-round-blue-cell picture described here.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Leiomyosarcoma is a smooth-muscle malignant tumour without the cambium layer or strap cells described.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Osteosarcoma is a bone-forming malignant tumour, not the orbital small-round-blue-cell tumour described.
explanations.E: Correct. Progressive exophthalmos from a large orbital mass in a young child, with biopsy showing sheets of small round blue cells and spindle cells in myxoid stroma condensing into a cambium layer beneath the surface epithelium, plus strap cells, is the classic picture of embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma — the most common soft-tissue sarcoma of childhood, arising from primitive mesenchymal cells with skeletal-muscle differentiation. The orbit is one of its classic sites. Strap cells (elongated, cross-striated cells) confirm the rhabdomyoblastic differentiation.

questions.title: Diagnostic significance of tennis racket cells
questions.question: Tennis racket cells are one of the diagnostic criteria of one of the following tumours:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Chondrosarcoma is characterised by a chondroid (cartilage) matrix, not tennis-racket-shaped strap cells.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Fibrosarcoma is characterised by a herringbone pattern of fibroblastic spindle cells, not tennis-racket-shaped strap cells.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Leiomyosarcoma is characterised by cigar-shaped smooth-muscle nuclei, not tennis-racket-shaped strap cells.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Osteosarcoma is characterised by malignant osteoid production, not tennis-racket-shaped strap cells.
explanations.E: Correct. Tennis-racket-shaped strap cells — elongated cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm, sometimes showing cross-striations — reflect skeletal muscle (rhabdomyoblastic) differentiation and are a specific diagnostic microscopic feature of rhabdomyosarcoma, not shared by the other sarcomas listed, which are built from cartilage, fibrous, smooth-muscle or bone-forming lineages instead. Finding these cells helps confirm the diagnosis when the clinical picture (paediatric small round blue cell tumour, cambium layer) is already suggestive.

questions.title: Genetic risk factor for squamous cell carcinoma
questions.question: One of the following is a genetic risk factor for squamous cell carcinoma:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Epstein-Barr virus is a viral, not genetic, risk factor, and is more classically linked to nasopharyngeal carcinoma and lymphoma than squamous cell carcinoma generally.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Human papillomavirus is a viral, not genetic, risk factor for squamous cell carcinoma.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Leukoplakia is a precursor lesion (a hyperkeratotic mucosal plaque), not itself a genetic risk factor.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Ultraviolet ray exposure is an environmental, not genetic, risk factor for squamous cell carcinoma.
explanations.E: Correct. Xeroderma pigmentosum is an inherited defect in nucleotide excision DNA repair that leaves UV-induced DNA damage unrepaired, making it the genetic (inherited) risk factor for squamous cell carcinoma among these options — distinct from the environmental (UV), viral (HPV, EBV) and precursor-lesion (leukoplakia) risk factors also listed. Because the defect is present from birth, affected patients develop skin cancers, including SCC, at a markedly younger age than the general population.

questions.title: Tumour type where microscopic criteria of malignancy apply best
questions.question: Microscopic criteria of malignancy are the features of one of the following tumours:

explanations.A: Correct. Standard microscopic criteria of malignancy — nuclear pleomorphism, hyperchromatism, increased and abnormal mitoses, loss of normal cell polarity — correlate well with aggressive behaviour in conventional carcinomas such as breast carcinoma, making them reliable grading features there. This reliability is the exception, not the rule, among the tumour types listed, all of which (clear cell renal cell carcinoma, papillary thyroid carcinoma, and neuroendocrine tumours of appendix or pancreas) are well-recognised exceptions where these same criteria do not reliably predict clinical behaviour. This is why breast carcinoma is the answer among the five options.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Clear cell renal cell carcinoma is one of the recognised exceptions where standard nuclear/mitotic criteria are unreliable for predicting behaviour; grading instead relies on nucleolar (Fuhrman/WHO/ISUP) grade.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Papillary thyroid carcinoma is diagnosed and graded mainly by nuclear features (e.g. Orphan Annie eyes, grooves) rather than the standard mitotic/pleomorphism criteria of malignancy.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A well-differentiated appendiceal neuroendocrine tumour can behave in a way that does not correlate well with standard cytological malignancy criteria; grading instead relies on mitotic count and Ki-67 index.
explanations.E: Incorrect. A pancreatic neuroendocrine tumour similarly does not reliably follow standard cytological malignancy criteria; tumour-specific grading systems are used instead.

questions.title: Vaginal mass in a young girl, cambium layer
questions.question: A female child, 3 years old, has progressive vaginal discharge. Radiology revealed a large vaginal mass. Biopsy revealed sheets of small round blue cells admixed with spindle-shaped cells in a myxoid stroma condensed underneath the surface epithelium (cambium layer). Occasional large spindle-shaped cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm were identified. What is your diagnosis?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Chondrosarcoma is a cartilage-forming malignant tumour, not the small-round-blue-cell/cambium-layer picture described.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Fibrosarcoma is a fibroblastic spindle-cell tumour without the cambium layer or eosinophilic strap-cell-type cells described.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Leiomyosarcoma is a smooth-muscle malignant tumour without the cambium layer described here.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Osteosarcoma is a bone-forming malignant tumour, not the vaginal small-round-blue-cell tumour described.
explanations.E: Correct. A vaginal mass in a young girl with progressive discharge, biopsy showing small round blue cells and spindle cells in myxoid stroma condensing into a cambium layer beneath the epithelium, plus large eosinophilic (strap-like) cells, is the classic picture of embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma presenting as sarcoma botryoides — the grape-like vaginal presentation of this tumour in young children. This is the same tumour and underlying fact as the orbital-mass vignette elsewhere in this exam, tested here at its other classic site.
